not because of strength or technique, but because their socks slip.

That’s the problem our Grip Socks were built to solve.

By locking your foot in place inside the skate, they improve energy transfer, stability, and control - shift after shift - while reducing unnecessary friction.

No slipping. No twisting. No blisters. No wasted power.
Once you feel the difference, regular socks won’t cut it anymore.

Please STOP telling yourself it's just your age. I'm 37. If your feet feel worse after hockey than they used to, it might not be your skates. It's probably what's between your foot and the boot.

Buying thicker socks didn't fix it for me.

I've been playing beer league for over 15 years.

For the last two seasons, this is what my body kept telling me: "My feet go numb by the second period." "My ankles feel wrecked walking to the car after a game." "I get blisters no matter what socks I buy." "Maybe I'm just getting too old for this."

Before I gave up another Tuesday night, I actually looked at what was going on inside my skate.

I pulled my socks off after a game and looked at them properly for the first time in years.

Flat. Sweaty. Zero grip left — if they ever had any to begin with.

I'd bought new skates that year. Broke them in properly. Even tried different insoles. But the one thing actually touching my foot never changed.

That was the mistake.

A regular sock feels fine going on. Soft, familiar. But your foot needs to stay locked in one position inside that boot, stride after stride — and a regular sock doesn't grip anything. It just lets your foot move.

Every stride, force travels from your push-off, through your foot, into the boot. If your foot shifts even a little inside there, some of that force turns into friction instead of speed. Into blisters instead of power. Into your ankle working overtime just to keep you stable.

One shift isn't the problem. But a season is hundreds of shifts. My feet were absorbing all of it, every single game.

At first it was small. Feet feeling hot by the second period. Heel tender the next day. Then it became a pattern — double up on socks, lace tighter, tape my heel before every game, sit out the second half of back-to-backs.

I started saying no to games I used to say yes to.

I told myself it was age.

It wasn't. My skates weren't the problem. What was between my foot and the boot was.

Doubling up on socks tricked me for a while — feet felt padded again, problem solved, or so I thought. But it was the same ungripped surface underneath, just with an extra layer. Like putting a second bald tire on top of the first one. More rubber, same grip.

So I switched to RocketGrip Hockey Grip Socks.

They've got silicone grip zones right at the heel, ankle, and arch — the exact spots where my foot used to slide. Instead of a flat sock just sitting there, it actually grips the inside of the boot when I push off.

You put them on exactly like a normal sock. Same fit I'm used to. I just upgraded what's happening underneath.

First game wearing them, I noticed it on the hard stops — my foot just wasn't moving around in there anymore. No hot spot building by the second period. No taping my heel beforehand.

The part I didn't expect: I stopped lacing my skates so tight. I used to crank them down hard because my foot felt unstable — that was me compensating. Once my foot was actually locked in, I didn't need to strangle it with the laces on top. My feet don't go numb nearly as fast now.

I'm not going to tell you this turned me into a faster skater. It's not a replacement for skates that actually fit you, and it's not a medical fix. It's one less thing working against your foot every stride.

Once you're past 35, recovery matters as much as performance. The goal isn't just playing well tonight — it's still wanting to lace up next season, and in five years.

Nobody markets hockey gear around this. It's always more speed, more power, lighter equipment. For guys like me, the actual advantage is just being able to keep showing up — playing back-to-back nights, finishing a game without my ankle feeling wrecked, playing Tuesday and still wanting to play Thursday.

RocketGrip works with any skate, any brand, whatever fit you already play in — recreational or competitive. You just wear them like a normal sock and lace up the way you always do. No new skates, no new insoles, nothing to relearn.

Before you buy another pack of thick socks, before you blame your skates, before you decide sore feet are just the price of playing past 35 — pull off your sock after your next game and actually look at it.

It might still look fine. It might not be doing its job anymore.

STOP blaming your skates. Upgrade the layer that actually holds your foot in place.

Try RocketGrip Hockey Grip Socks: 👉 rocketgrip.com/products/custom-hockey-grip-socks

P.S. They go on just like a normal sock — same skates, same lacing, just a better foundation underneath.

P.P.S. Don't wait until sore feet or ankle instability start deciding how often you play. I wish I'd switched two seasons earlier.

P.P.P.S. Persistent foot, ankle, or joint pain should be assessed by an appropriate healthcare professional.

body.text:
I make every tennis player over 35 do this one thing—and most of them have never heard of it.

I’ve coached tennis for more than 20 years.

And I’ve watched the same story happen again and again.

A player reaches their late 30s, 40s or 50s.

They still love the game.

They still want to compete.

Their technique may be better than it was ten years ago.

But their body no longer recovers the same way.

First, their wrist feels slightly sore after a long session.

Then the outside of the elbow starts bothering them.

They begin wearing a brace.
They ice their arm after matches.
They stop serving at full speed.
They avoid playing on consecutive days.

Eventually, a player who once played four times per week is happy if they can get through one session without discomfort.

And in many cases, they blame age.
They tell themselves:
“I’m just getting older.”
“My arm can’t handle tennis anymore.”
“Maybe it’s time to play less.”

But age isn’t always the whole problem.

Sometimes the equipment is repeatedly sending unnecessary stress into the same joints, shot after shot, session after session.

And almost nobody pays attention to the part of the racket responsible for absorbing it.

Every time you hit a tennis ball, the collision creates vibration.

That vibration travels through the racket head.
Down the frame.
Into the handle.

Then directly into your hand, wrist, forearm and elbow.

One shot doesn’t feel like much.

Neither does one vibration.

But during a normal tennis session, you might strike hundreds of balls.
Forehands.
Backhands.
Volleys.
Serves.
Returns.

And if you play several times per week, that means your arm is absorbing thousands of small impacts every month.

For a younger player, recovery may happen quickly.

But as you get older, accumulated stress starts to matter more.

Your tendons may take longer to recover.

Your joints may feel stiffer the next morning.

Small aches can remain between sessions instead of disappearing overnight.

That is how players quietly lose years on the court.

It usually doesn’t happen through one dramatic injury.

It happens gradually.

They start shortening sessions.

Then they stop serving.

Then they take a few weeks off.

Then a few months.

Eventually, the racket stays in the bag.

I’ve watched players leave the sport who could have enjoyed another five or ten good years of tennis.

Not because they lost their love for the game.

Because playing became too uncomfortable.

And here’s the frustrating part:
Most players try to solve this by changing the wrong things.
They buy a softer string.
They lower their string tension.
They switch to a heavier racket.
Then a lighter racket.
They buy a vibration dampener.
They replace their overgrip.

Some of those changes can help.

But almost nobody looks underneath the overgrip.

Your overgrip controls the surface feel.
It can provide tack.
It can absorb sweat.
It can make the handle feel fresh.
But beneath it is the base grip—the layer sitting directly between your hand and the hard racket handle.

And most standard base grips are made from foam or synthetic materials that gradually compress.

Over time, that cushioning flattens.
The grip begins to feel harder.
Less responsive.
Less protective.

So even if you put a brand-new overgrip on top, the worn foundation underneath is still transmitting vibration into your arm.

You’re replacing the surface while ignoring the layer responsible for cushioning the impact.

That’s why I now put an Octopus Tennis Undergrip on my students’ rackets.

It isn’t another overgrip.

It replaces the standard base grip underneath your normal overgrip.

The Octopus is made from flexible silicone with a raised, shock-absorbing structure.

When the racket vibrates after impact, the silicone bumps compress.

They help absorb that vibration before as much of it reaches your hand, wrist and elbow.

Then the silicone rebounds instead of remaining permanently flattened like ordinary foam.

You still wrap your favourite overgrip on top.

So you keep the tack, texture and surface feel you already prefer.

But underneath it, you have a more protective and responsive foundation.

That distinction is important.

Your overgrip helps you hold the racket.

Your undergrip helps manage what the racket sends back into your arm.

The first thing many players notice is comfort.

The racket feels less harsh when they make imperfect contact.

Off-centre shots don’t feel as aggressive through the handle.

Long hitting sessions become easier on the hand and forearm.

But comfort isn’t the only reason I recommend it.

When a racket feels harsh or unstable, players instinctively grip it harder.
They tighten their fingers.
Their wrist becomes rigid.
Their forearm stays tense through the swing.
They may not even realize they’re doing it.
But that tension affects performance.

A tight hand makes it harder for the racket head to flow naturally.
You lose acceleration.
You lose touch.
You become tentative on full swings.
And the more tired your arm becomes, the tighter you hold the racket.

It becomes a cycle:
The racket feels harsh.
You grip harder.
Your arm becomes more tense.
The racket feels even harsher.

A more comfortable and stable handle can help you trust the racket again.

You don’t need to squeeze it as though it’s about to fly out of your hand.
Your wrist can stay looser.
Your swing can remain smoother.

And you can focus on the ball instead of thinking about your elbow.

That is why my students don’t only tell me the racket feels more comfortable.

They often say they feel more confident accelerating through the shot.
They feel more connected to the handle.
They stop making constant adjustments between points.
They can play longer before their hand and forearm feel exhausted.
And they stop arriving at lessons with ice wrapped around their elbow.

The Octopus doesn’t teach technique.
It doesn’t replace proper coaching.
And it can’t turn a beginner into a professional player.

What it does is remove an unnecessary source of harshness between the racket and your arm.
That gives your technique a better platform.

Because good technique is much harder to maintain when you’re protecting a sore wrist.
It’s difficult to swing freely when you’re anticipating elbow discomfort.

And no coach can get your best tennis out of you if your main concern is simply finishing the session without pain.

The Octopus works with:
→ Any standard tennis racket
→ Any racket brand
→ Your preferred overgrip
→ Recreational and competitive setups
→ Players who want comfort without losing racket feel

Installation is simple.
Remove the old base grip.
Roll the Octopus undergrip onto the handle using the application tool.
Then wrap your usual overgrip over it.

You don’t have to change your racket.
You don’t have to abandon the overgrip you already love.
And you don’t have to make the handle feel excessively padded or disconnected.
You’re simply upgrading the hidden layer underneath.

This is especially worth considering if:
→ You’re over 35 and play regularly
→ Your wrist or elbow feels tired after tennis
→ Off-centre shots feel harsh through the handle
→ You’ve started wearing a wrist or elbow brace
→ You need more recovery time between sessions
→ You grip the racket tighter as you get tired
→ Your existing base grip feels flat, hard or compressed
→ You want to continue playing several times per week
→ Staying on the court matters more to you than buying another new racket

Most tennis products promise more spin.
More power.
More control.

Those benefits are easy to advertise.

But at a certain point in your tennis life, the most valuable performance benefit is different:
Being able to play again tomorrow.
Then again next week.
And again ten years from now.

Because the best racket setup isn’t only the one that helps you hit harder today.

It’s the one that helps you keep playing the sport you love.

If you’re serious about staying on the court, look beneath your overgrip.

The small impacts you barely notice today may be the reason you’re forced to play less in the future.

The Octopus Undergrip helps create a more comfortable, stable and shock-absorbing connection between your hand and the racket.
Same racket.
Same overgrip.
Same player.
But a much better foundation for the years ahead.

Try the Octopus Tennis Undergrip today:
👉 rocketgrip.com/products/tennis-undergrip

P.S. You don’t need to wait until your elbow becomes a serious problem. Equipment changes are most useful before discomfort forces you to stop playing.

P.P.S. The Octopus is installed beneath your regular overgrip. You keep the surface feel you already like while upgrading the cushioning and vibration management underneath.

P.P.P.S. The Octopus is not a medical treatment. Persistent wrist, elbow or forearm pain should be assessed by an appropriate medical professional.

body.text:
Please STOP putting a fresh overgrip on top of a dead base grip.

If you’re over 35 and your wrist or elbow feels worse after tennis than it used to, your racket may be sending far more vibration into your arm than you realize.

And replacing the overgrip won’t fix it.

I’ve coached tennis for over 20 years.

Whenever a player tells me:
“My elbow is starting to bother me.”
“My wrist feels beaten up after longer matches.”
“I can’t play two days in a row anymore.”
“I think I’m getting too old for tennis.”

I check one thing before we discuss a new racket, new strings or another brace.

I peel back their overgrip.

And underneath, I usually find the same thing.

A flattened, compressed base grip that stopped doing its job months—or even years—ago.

The player has replaced the outer grip ten times.

But the layer responsible for cushioning every impact has never been touched.

That’s the mistake.

Your overgrip is only the surface.
It gives you tack.
It absorbs sweat.
It makes the handle feel fresh.

But underneath that thin layer is the base grip sitting directly between your hand and the hard racket handle.

And every time you strike the ball, vibration travels:
From the strings…
Through the racket frame…
Down the handle…
Into your palm, wrist, forearm and elbow.

One shot isn’t the problem.

But tennis is not one shot.

It’s hundreds of impacts in a single session.
Thousands every month.
Year after year.

And when the foam beneath your overgrip becomes compressed, it absorbs less of that vibration.

So your arm absorbs more.

At first, you barely notice it.
Your forearm feels slightly tired after playing.
Your wrist is stiff the next morning.
Your elbow takes longer to warm up.

Then you begin making small adjustments.
You grip the racket tighter.
You avoid serving at full speed.
You stop hitting your backhand freely.
You wear a brace.
You ice your elbow after playing.
You take an extra day off between sessions.

Eventually, the player who once played four times per week is nervous about playing twice.

And they blame their age.

But the problem may not be that their body suddenly became incapable of tennis.

Their equipment may simply have stopped protecting them from the repeated impact.

That is why putting on another overgrip can be misleading.
The racket feels fresh again.
The handle feels tackier.

For a few sessions, you think the problem is solved.

But the same hard, compressed foundation is still sitting underneath.

It’s like putting a new mattress cover over a mattress that has completely collapsed.
The surface looks better.
The support underneath hasn’t changed.

That’s why I now recommend the Octopus Tennis Undergrip to players who are serious about staying on the court.

It replaces the standard foam base grip beneath your normal overgrip.

Instead of relying on foam that gradually flattens, the Octopus uses a flexible silicone structure with raised cushioning points.

When the racket vibrates after impact, the silicone compresses.

It helps absorb the vibration before as much of it reaches your arm.
Then it rebounds.
That rebound matters.

Traditional foam gradually becomes flatter and harder.

The silicone structure is designed to keep responding instead of simply staying compressed.

You then wrap your favourite overgrip on top.

So you don’t have to change the tack, texture or surface feel you already like.
You keep your normal overgrip.
You upgrade the hidden foundation beneath it.

The first time many players use it, they notice that the racket feels less harsh.
Especially on imperfect contact.
You know the shot.
You catch the ball slightly late.
Or too close to the frame.

The racket sends a sharp sensation directly into your hand.
With a better layer beneath the grip, that impact feels more controlled.
Less aggressive.
More cushioned without making the racket feel soft or disconnected.

But there’s another benefit players often don’t expect.

They stop squeezing the racket so hard.

When your handle feels unstable or harsh, your body naturally tries to protect itself.
Your fingers tighten.
Your wrist becomes rigid.
Your forearm stays tense through the swing.

That tension may help you feel secure for a moment.

But it can also reduce racket-head speed, touch and fluidity.
You start fighting the racket instead of swinging it.

A more comfortable and stable foundation helps you hold the handle securely without strangling it.
Your hand can stay looser.
Your wrist can move more naturally.
Your forearm doesn’t need to remain tense through every shot.
And your attention can return to the ball instead of the discomfort in your elbow.

This is not about turning you into a professional player.
It’s not a replacement for technique.

And it’s not a medical treatment.
It’s a simple equipment change designed to reduce one unnecessary source of stress between your racket and your arm.

Because once you reach your late 30s, 40s or 50s, recovery matters.

The goal isn’t only to play well today.

It’s to still be playing tomorrow.
Next season.
And ten years from now.

Most tennis marketing focuses on:
More spin.
More power.
More control.

But for many experienced players, the most valuable performance advantage is being able to keep showing up.
To finish a match without immediately reaching for the ice pack.
To serve freely instead of protecting the elbow.
To play on Saturday and still feel capable of playing again on Sunday.

That’s tennis longevity.

And it often starts with reducing the repeated stress your body absorbs from every shot.

The Octopus Undergrip works with:
→ Standard tennis rackets
→ Any racket brand
→ Your preferred overgrip
→ Recreational and competitive setups
→ Players who want more cushioning without losing feel

Installation is straightforward.
Remove the old base grip.
Roll the Octopus onto the racket handle using the included application tool.
Then wrap your normal overgrip over it.

You don’t need to buy a new racket.
You don’t need to change your strings.
You don’t need to abandon the grip texture you already prefer.
You simply replace the worn-out layer nobody thinks about.

So before you buy another pack of overgrips…

Before you blame your racket…

And before you decide that wrist and elbow discomfort are simply the price of getting older…

Look underneath.

Your overgrip may still look fine.

But the base grip beneath it may have stopped protecting you a long time ago.

STOP covering the problem with another overgrip.

Upgrade the layer that absorbs the impact.

Try the Octopus Tennis Undergrip:
👉 rocketgrip.com/products/tennis-undergrip

P.S. The Octopus sits beneath your regular overgrip. You keep the outer feel you already like while upgrading the cushioning and vibration management underneath.

P.P.S. Don’t wait until discomfort forces you to stop playing. The best time to protect your future years on the court is while you’re still able to enjoy them.

P.P.P.S. Persistent wrist, elbow or forearm pain should be assessed by an appropriate healthcare professional.

STOP blaming your skates for feet that go numb by the second period.

If you're over 35 and hockey doesn't feel the same on your feet as it used to, the issue usually isn't the skates. It's what's between your foot and the boot.

And another pair of thick socks won't fix it.

Ask any long-time rec-league player over 35 what's changed, and you'll hear some version of the same four things: "My feet go numb by the second period." "My ankles feel wrecked by the third." "I get blisters no matter what socks I wear." "Maybe I'm just getting too old for this."

It's rarely the skates. Most players have broken in a new pair, tried different insoles, changed their lacing — and the problem stays exactly the same.

That's because the one layer actually touching the foot usually never changes: a regular sock, cotton or basic athletic, never built to handle what happens inside a hockey boot.

Here's what's actually happening.

Your foot needs to stay locked in one position inside the boot, stride after stride. A regular sock doesn't grip anything — it just sits there, and lets the foot move.

Every stride, force travels from the push-off, through the foot, into the boot. If the foot shifts even a few millimeters inside that boot, some of that force turns into friction instead of stride power. Into blisters instead of speed. Into the ankle working overtime to stabilize what the sock isn't holding in place.

One stride isn't the issue. A season is thousands of them.

And when a sock has zero grip, the foot moves a little more with every single one. First it's a hot spot by the second period. Then a tender heel the next morning. Then a "loose" feeling ankle by the third.

The usual fixes — doubling up on socks, lacing tighter, taping the heel before every game — treat the symptom, not the cause. The foot feels padded again for a game or two. But the same ungripped surface is still sitting between the foot and the boot. It's a second bald tire on top of the first one — more rubber, same grip.

RocketGrip Hockey Grip Socks fix the actual cause.

Silicone grip zones sit at the heel, ankle, and arch — the exact points where a regular sock lets the foot slide. When the foot pushes off, the silicone grips the inside of the boot instead of letting it travel.

They go on exactly like a normal sock. Same fit, same feel. Only what's happening at the foot-boot interface changes.

Players also tend to stop lacing their skates so aggressively tight. An unstable foot gets compensated for with tighter laces — which cuts circulation and adds its own pressure points. A foot that's already locked in doesn't need to be strangled on top of it. Circulation stays better. Numbness shows up later, or not at all.

This isn't a performance gimmick and it isn't a medical treatment. It's a simple equipment change that removes one unnecessary source of friction between the foot and the boot.

Because past your mid-30s, recovery matters as much as performance. The goal isn't just playing well tonight — it's still lacing up next season, and in five years.

Most hockey gear is marketed on speed and power. For a lot of recreational players, the real advantage is simpler: being able to keep showing up. Back-to-back games without taping your feet beforehand. Finishing a game without your ankle feeling wrecked. Playing Tuesday and still wanting to play Thursday.

RocketGrip Hockey Grip Socks work with: → Any skate → Any brand → Regular or custom fit → Recreational and competitive players → Anyone who wants a locked-in feel without changing their skates

Wearing them is simple: pull them on like a normal sock, lace up the way you always do. No new skates, no new insoles, nothing to relearn.

Before buying another pair of thick socks, before blaming the skates, before deciding sore feet are just the price of playing past 35 — look at what's actually between the foot and the boot.

It might still look fine. It may have stopped doing its job a long time ago.

STOP blaming the skates. Upgrade the layer that actually holds the foot in place.

Shop RocketGrip Hockey Grip Socks: 👉 rocketgrip.com/products/custom-hockey-grip-socks

P.S. They go on just like a normal sock — same skates, same lacing, just a better foundation underneath.

P.P.S. Don't wait until sore feet or ankle instability start limiting how often you play.

P.P.P.S. Persistent foot, ankle, or joint pain should be assessed by an appropriate healthcare professional.

Please STOP putting a fresh overgrip on top of a dead base grip.

If you’re over 35 and your wrist or elbow feels worse after tennis than it used to, your racket may be sending far more vibration into your arm than you realize.

And replacing the overgrip won’t fix it.

I’ve coached tennis for over 20 years.

Whenever a player tells me:
“My elbow is starting to bother me.”
“My wrist feels beaten up after longer matches.”
“I can’t play two days in a row anymore.”
“I think I’m getting too old for tennis.”

I check one thing before we discuss a new racket, new strings or another brace.

I peel back their overgrip.

And underneath, I usually find the same thing.

A flattened, compressed base grip that stopped doing its job months—or even years—ago.

The player has replaced the outer grip ten times.

But the layer responsible for cushioning every impact has never been touched.

That’s the mistake.

Your overgrip is only the surface.
It gives you tack.
It absorbs sweat.
It makes the handle feel fresh.

But underneath that thin layer is the base grip sitting directly between your hand and the hard racket handle.

And every time you strike the ball, vibration travels:
From the strings…
Through the racket frame…
Down the handle…
Into your palm, wrist, forearm and elbow.

One shot isn’t the problem.

But tennis is not one shot.

It’s hundreds of impacts in a single session.
Thousands every month.
Year after year.

And when the foam beneath your overgrip becomes compressed, it absorbs less of that vibration.

So your arm absorbs more.

At first, you barely notice it.
Your forearm feels slightly tired after playing.
Your wrist is stiff the next morning.
Your elbow takes longer to warm up.

Then you begin making small adjustments.
You grip the racket tighter.
You avoid serving at full speed.
You stop hitting your backhand freely.
You wear a brace.
You ice your elbow after playing.
You take an extra day off between sessions.

Eventually, the player who once played four times per week is nervous about playing twice.

And they blame their age.

But the problem may not be that their body suddenly became incapable of tennis.

Their equipment may simply have stopped protecting them from the repeated impact.

That is why putting on another overgrip can be misleading.
The racket feels fresh again.
The handle feels tackier.

For a few sessions, you think the problem is solved.

But the same hard, compressed foundation is still sitting underneath.

It’s like putting a new mattress cover over a mattress that has completely collapsed.
The surface looks better.
The support underneath hasn’t changed.

That’s why I now recommend the Octopus Tennis Undergrip to players who are serious about staying on the court.

It replaces the standard foam base grip beneath your normal overgrip.

Instead of relying on foam that gradually flattens, the Octopus uses a flexible silicone structure with raised cushioning points.

When the racket vibrates after impact, the silicone compresses.

It helps absorb the vibration before as much of it reaches your arm.
Then it rebounds.
That rebound matters.

Traditional foam gradually becomes flatter and harder.

The silicone structure is designed to keep responding instead of simply staying compressed.

You then wrap your favourite overgrip on top.

So you don’t have to change the tack, texture or surface feel you already like.
You keep your normal overgrip.
You upgrade the hidden foundation beneath it.

The first time many players use it, they notice that the racket feels less harsh.
Especially on imperfect contact.
You know the shot.
You catch the ball slightly late.
Or too close to the frame.

The racket sends a sharp sensation directly into your hand.
With a better layer beneath the grip, that impact feels more controlled.
Less aggressive.
More cushioned without making the racket feel soft or disconnected.

But there’s another benefit players often don’t expect.

They stop squeezing the racket so hard.

When your handle feels unstable or harsh, your body naturally tries to protect itself.
Your fingers tighten.
Your wrist becomes rigid.
Your forearm stays tense through the swing.

That tension may help you feel secure for a moment.

But it can also reduce racket-head speed, touch and fluidity.
You start fighting the racket instead of swinging it.

A more comfortable and stable foundation helps you hold the handle securely without strangling it.
Your hand can stay looser.
Your wrist can move more naturally.
Your forearm doesn’t need to remain tense through every shot.
And your attention can return to the ball instead of the discomfort in your elbow.

This is not about turning you into a professional player.
It’s not a replacement for technique.

And it’s not a medical treatment.
It’s a simple equipment change designed to reduce one unnecessary source of stress between your racket and your arm.

Because once you reach your late 30s, 40s or 50s, recovery matters.

The goal isn’t only to play well today.

It’s to still be playing tomorrow.
Next season.
And ten years from now.

Most tennis marketing focuses on:
More spin.
More power.
More control.

But for many experienced players, the most valuable performance advantage is being able to keep showing up.
To finish a match without immediately reaching for the ice pack.
To serve freely instead of protecting the elbow.
To play on Saturday and still feel capable of playing again on Sunday.

That’s tennis longevity.

And it often starts with reducing the repeated stress your body absorbs from every shot.

The Octopus Undergrip works with:
→ Standard tennis rackets
→ Any racket brand
→ Your preferred overgrip
→ Recreational and competitive setups
→ Players who want more cushioning without losing feel

Installation is straightforward.
Remove the old base grip.
Roll the Octopus onto the racket handle using the included application tool.
Then wrap your normal overgrip over it.

You don’t need to buy a new racket.
You don’t need to change your strings.
You don’t need to abandon the grip texture you already prefer.
You simply replace the worn-out layer nobody thinks about.

So before you buy another pack of overgrips…

Before you blame your racket…

And before you decide that wrist and elbow discomfort are simply the price of getting older…

Look underneath.

Your overgrip may still look fine.

But the base grip beneath it may have stopped protecting you a long time ago.

STOP covering the problem with another overgrip.

Upgrade the layer that absorbs the impact.

Try the Octopus Tennis Undergrip:
👉 rocketgrip.com/products/tennis-undergrip

P.S. The Octopus sits beneath your regular overgrip. You keep the outer feel you already like while upgrading the cushioning and vibration management underneath.

P.P.S. Don’t wait until discomfort forces you to stop playing. The best time to protect your future years on the court is while you’re still able to enjoy them.

P.P.P.S. Persistent wrist, elbow or forearm pain should be assessed by an appropriate healthcare professional.

Please STOP telling yourself it's just your age. I'm 37. If your feet feel worse after hockey than they used to, it might not be your skates. It's probably what's between your foot and the boot.

Buying thicker socks didn't fix it for me.

I've been playing beer league for over 15 years.

For the last two seasons, this is what my body kept telling me: "My feet go numb by the second period." "My ankles feel wrecked walking to the car after a game." "I get blisters no matter what socks I buy." "Maybe I'm just getting too old for this."

Before I gave up another Tuesday night, I actually looked at what was going on inside my skate.

I pulled my socks off after a game and looked at them properly for the first time in years.

Flat. Sweaty. Zero grip left — if they ever had any to begin with.

I'd bought new skates that year. Broke them in properly. Even tried different insoles. But the one thing actually touching my foot never changed.

That was the mistake.

A regular sock feels fine going on. Soft, familiar. But your foot needs to stay locked in one position inside that boot, stride after stride — and a regular sock doesn't grip anything. It just lets your foot move.

Every stride, force travels from your push-off, through your foot, into the boot. If your foot shifts even a little inside there, some of that force turns into friction instead of speed. Into blisters instead of power. Into your ankle working overtime just to keep you stable.

Please STOP putting a fresh overgrip on top of a dead base grip.

If you’re over 35 and your wrist or elbow feels worse after tennis than it used to, your racket may be sending far more vibration into your arm than you realize.

And replacing the overgrip won’t fix it.

I’ve coached tennis for over 20 years.

Whenever a player tells me:
“My elbow is starting to bother me.”
“My wrist feels beaten up after longer matches.”
“I can’t play two days in a row anymore.”
“I think I’m getting too old for tennis.”

I check one thing before we discuss a new racket, new strings or another brace.

I peel back their overgrip.

And underneath, I usually find the same thing.

A flattened, compressed base grip that stopped doing its job months—or even years—ago.

The player has replaced the outer grip ten times.

But the layer responsible for cushioning every impact has never been touched.

That’s the mistake.

Your overgrip is only the surface.
It gives you tack.
It absorbs sweat.
It makes the handle feel fresh.

But underneath that thin layer is the base grip sitting directly between your hand and the hard racket handle.

And every time you strike the ball, vibration travels:
From the strings…
Through the racket frame…
Down the handle…
Into your palm, wrist, forearm and elbow.

One shot isn’t the problem.

But tennis is not one shot.

It’s hundreds of impacts in a single session.
Thousands every month.
Year after year.

And when the foam beneath your overgrip becomes compressed, it absorbs less of that vibration.

So your arm absorbs more.

At first, you barely notice it.
Your forearm feels slightly tired after playing.
Your wrist is stiff the next morning.
Your elbow takes longer to warm up.

Then you begin making small adjustments.
You grip the racket tighter.
You avoid serving at full speed.
You stop hitting your backhand freely.
You wear a brace.
You ice your elbow after playing.
You take an extra day off between sessions.

Eventually, the player who once played four times per week is nervous about playing twice.

And they blame their age.

But the problem may not be that their body suddenly became incapable of tennis.

Their equipment may simply have stopped protecting them from the repeated impact.

That is why putting on another overgrip can be misleading.
The racket feels fresh again.
The handle feels tackier.

For a few sessions, you think the problem is solved.

But the same hard, compressed foundation is still sitting underneath.

It’s like putting a new mattress cover over a mattress that has completely collapsed.
The surface looks better.
The support underneath hasn’t changed.

That’s why I now recommend the Octopus Tennis Undergrip to players who are serious about staying on the court.

It replaces the standard foam base grip beneath your normal overgrip.

Instead of relying on foam that gradually flattens, the Octopus uses a flexible silicone structure with raised cushioning points.

When the racket vibrates after impact, the silicone compresses.

It helps absorb the vibration before as much of it reaches your arm.
Then it rebounds.
That rebound matters.

Traditional foam gradually becomes flatter and harder.

The silicone structure is designed to keep responding instead of simply staying compressed.

You then wrap your favourite overgrip on top.

So you don’t have to change the tack, texture or surface feel you already like.
You keep your normal overgrip.
You upgrade the hidden foundation beneath it.

The first time many players use it, they notice that the racket feels less harsh.
Especially on imperfect contact.
You know the shot.
You catch the ball slightly late.
Or too close to the frame.

The racket sends a sharp sensation directly into your hand.
With a better layer beneath the grip, that impact feels more controlled.
Less aggressive.
More cushioned without making the racket feel soft or disconnected.

But there’s another benefit players often don’t expect.

They stop squeezing the racket so hard.

When your handle feels unstable or harsh, your body naturally tries to protect itself.
Your fingers tighten.
Your wrist becomes rigid.
Your forearm stays tense through the swing.

But it can also reduce racket-head speed, touch and fluidity.
You start fighting the racket instead of swinging it.

A more comfortable and stable foundation helps you hold the handle securely without strangling it.
Your hand can stay looser.
Your wrist can move more naturally.
Your forearm doesn’t need to remain tense through every shot.
And your attention can return to the ball instead of the discomfort in your elbow.

This is not about turning you into a professional player.
It’s not a replacement for technique.

And it’s not a medical treatment.
It’s a simple equipment change designed to reduce one unnecessary source of stress between your racket and your arm.

Because once you reach your late 30s, 40s or 50s, recovery matters.

The goal isn’t only to play well today.

It’s to still be playing tomorrow.
Next season.
And ten years from now.

More spin.
More power.
More control.

To finish a match without immediately reaching for the ice pack.
To serve freely instead of protecting the elbow.
To play on Saturday and still feel capable of playing again on Sunday.

That’s tennis longevity.

And it often starts with reducing the repeated stress your body absorbs from every shot.

The Octopus Undergrip works with:
→ Standard tennis rackets
→ Any racket brand
→ Your preferred overgrip
→ Recreational and competitive setups
→ Players who want more cushioning without losing feel

Installation is straightforward.
Remove the old base grip.
Roll the Octopus onto the racket handle using the included application tool.
Then wrap your normal overgrip over it.

You don’t need to buy a new racket.
You don’t need to change your strings.
You don’t need to abandon the grip texture you already prefer.
You simply replace the worn-out layer nobody thinks about.

So before you buy another pack of overgrips…

Before you blame your racket…

And before you decide that wrist and elbow discomfort are simply the price of getting older…

Look underneath.

Your overgrip may still look fine.

But the base grip beneath it may have stopped protecting you a long time ago.

STOP covering the problem with another overgrip.

Upgrade the layer that absorbs the impact.

Try the Octopus Tennis Undergrip:
👉 rocketgrip.com/products/tennis-undergrip

P.S. The Octopus sits beneath your regular overgrip. You keep the outer feel you already like while upgrading the cushioning and vibration management underneath.

cards.body:
Please STOP blaming your skates for feet that go numb by the second period.

If you're over 35 and your feet feel worse after hockey than they used to, your skates probably aren't the problem. It's what's between your foot and the boot.

And a thicker pair of socks won't fix it.

I've coached hockey for over 20 years.

Whenever a player tells me: "My feet go numb by the second period." "My ankles feel wrecked by the third." "I get blisters no matter what socks I wear." "I think I'm getting too old to play three times a week."

I check one thing before we talk about new skates, new insoles, or another brace.

I ask what's actually on their foot.

And underneath the skate, I usually find the same thing.

A regular sock — cotton, basic athletic, whatever was in the drawer — that was never built to handle what happens inside a hockey boot.

The player has broken in two new pairs of skates. Tried different lacing. Added insoles. But the one layer that actually touches his foot has never changed.

That's the mistake.

Your sock feels soft. Familiar. Like a sock should.

But between your foot and the hard shell of the boot, your foot needs to stay locked in exactly one position, stride after stride. A regular sock doesn't grip anything. It just sits there — and lets your foot travel.

Every stride you take, force moves: From your push-off… Through your foot… Into the boot…

And if your foot shifts even a few millimeters inside that boot, some of that force doesn't go into your stride. It goes into friction. Into your skin. Into your ankle working overtime to stabilize what your sock isn't holding in place.

One stride isn't the problem.

But hockey is not one stride.

It's dozens of hard pushes in a single shift. Hundreds in a game. Thousands across a season.

And when your sock has zero grip, your foot moves a little more with every one of them. So your skin absorbs more. Your ankle works harder.

At first, you barely notice it. Your feet feel a little hot by the second period. Your heel feels tender after a long practice. Your ankle feels "loose" by the third.

Then you start making small adjustments. You double up on socks. You lace your skates tighter. You tape your heel before every game. You bring a spare pair "just in case." You start sitting out the second game of a back-to-back.

Eventually, the guy who used to play three nights a week is nervous about two.

And he blames his age.

But the problem may not be that his body suddenly can't handle hockey anymore. His equipment may simply have stopped holding his foot in place.

That's why doubling up on socks can be misleading. Your foot feels padded again. For a game or two, you think the problem's solved.

But the same slippery, ungripped surface is still sitting between your foot and the boot.

It's like putting a second bald tire on top of the first one. It looks like more rubber. It doesn't grip any better.

That's why I now put RocketGrip Hockey Grip Socks on every player I coach who's serious about staying in the game.

Instead of plain fabric that just sits there, RocketGrip places silicone grip zones at the key contact points — heel, ankle, arch. When you push off, the silicone grips the inside of the boot and holds your foot in place, instead of letting it slide.

You put them on exactly like a normal sock. Same fit, same feel you're used to. You're just upgrading what's happening at the foot-boot interface.

The first time most players wear them, they notice it on the hard stops and starts — less shifting, a more secure ankle, no hot spot building by the second period.

But there's a second benefit players don't expect.

They stop lacing their skates so aggressively tight.

When your foot feels unstable inside the boot, you compensate by cranking your laces down harder to force some stability. 
That cuts circulation and adds pressure points of its own. A foot that's already locked in doesn't need to be strangled by the laces on top of it. Circulation stays better. Numbness shows up later, or not at all. And your attention goes back to the game instead of your feet.

This isn't about turning you into a faster skater overnight. It's not a replacement for properly fitted skates. And it's not a medical treatment. It's a simple equipment change designed to reduce one unnecessary source of friction between your foot and your boot.

Because once you're past your mid-30s, recovery matters. The goal isn't just playing well tonight. It's still lacing up next season. And in five years.

Most hockey gear marketing focuses on more speed, more power, lighter equipment. But for a lot of recreational players, the real advantage is simpler: being able to keep showing up. Playing back-to-back games without taping your feet beforehand. Finishing a game without your ankle feeling wrecked. Playing Tuesday and still wanting to play Thursday.

That's hockey longevity. And it often starts with what's happening inside your boot, not on the ice.

RocketGrip Hockey Grip Socks work with: → Any skate → Any brand → Regular or custom fit → Recreational and competitive players → Anyone who wants a locked-in feel without changing their skates

Wearing them is simple. Pull them on like a normal sock. Lace your skates the way you always do. That's it.

You don't need new skates. You don't need new insoles. You don't need to change how you lace. You just replace the layer between your foot and the boot that nobody thinks about.

So before you buy another pair of thick socks…

Before you blame your skates…

And before you decide that sore, numb feet are just the price of playing hockey past 35…

Look at what's actually between your foot and the boot.

Your feet might still feel "fine" for now. But the sock doing that job may have stopped protecting you a long time ago.

STOP blaming your skates. Upgrade the layer that actually holds your foot in place.

Try RocketGrip Hockey Grip Socks: 👉 rocketgrip.com/products/custom-hockey-grip-socks

P.S. RocketGrip socks go on just like a normal sock — you keep your usual skates and lacing, you're just upgrading what's happening underneath.

P.P.S. Don't wait until sore feet or ankle instability start limiting how often you play. The best time to fix this is while you're still lacing up regularly.

P.P.P.S. Persistent foot, ankle, or joint pain should be assessed by an appropriate healthcare professional.

body.text:
I make every tennis player over 35 do this one thing—and most of them have never heard of it.

I’ve coached tennis for more than 20 years.

And I’ve watched the same story happen again and again.

A player reaches their late 30s, 40s or 50s.

They still love the game.

They still want to compete.

Their technique may be better than it was ten years ago.

But their body no longer recovers the same way.

First, their wrist feels slightly sore after a long session.

Then the outside of the elbow starts bothering them.

They begin wearing a brace.
They ice their arm after matches.
They stop serving at full speed.
They avoid playing on consecutive days.

Eventually, a player who once played four times per week is happy if they can get through one session without discomfort.

And in many cases, they blame age.
They tell themselves:
“I’m just getting older.”
“My arm can’t handle tennis anymore.”
“Maybe it’s time to play less.”

But age isn’t always the whole problem.

Sometimes the equipment is repeatedly sending unnecessary stress into the same joints, shot after shot, session after session.

And almost nobody pays attention to the part of the racket responsible for absorbing it.

Every time you hit a tennis ball, the collision creates vibration.

That vibration travels through the racket head.
Down the frame.
Into the handle.

Then directly into your hand, wrist, forearm and elbow.

One shot doesn’t feel like much.

Neither does one vibration.

But during a normal tennis session, you might strike hundreds of balls.
Forehands.
Backhands.
Volleys.
Serves.
Returns.

And if you play several times per week, that means your arm is absorbing thousands of small impacts every month.

For a younger player, recovery may happen quickly.

But as you get older, accumulated stress starts to matter more.

Your tendons may take longer to recover.

Your joints may feel stiffer the next morning.

Small aches can remain between sessions instead of disappearing overnight.

That is how players quietly lose years on the court.

It usually doesn’t happen through one dramatic injury.

It happens gradually.

They start shortening sessions.

Then they stop serving.

Then they take a few weeks off.

Then a few months.

Eventually, the racket stays in the bag.

I’ve watched players leave the sport who could have enjoyed another five or ten good years of tennis.

Not because they lost their love for the game.

Because playing became too uncomfortable.

And here’s the frustrating part:
Most players try to solve this by changing the wrong things.
They buy a softer string.
They lower their string tension.
They switch to a heavier racket.
Then a lighter racket.
They buy a vibration dampener.
They replace their overgrip.

Some of those changes can help.

But almost nobody looks underneath the overgrip.

Your overgrip controls the surface feel.
It can provide tack.
It can absorb sweat.
It can make the handle feel fresh.
But beneath it is the base grip—the layer sitting directly between your hand and the hard racket handle.

And most standard base grips are made from foam or synthetic materials that gradually compress.

Over time, that cushioning flattens.
The grip begins to feel harder.
Less responsive.
Less protective.

So even if you put a brand-new overgrip on top, the worn foundation underneath is still transmitting vibration into your arm.

You’re replacing the surface while ignoring the layer responsible for cushioning the impact.

That’s why I now put an Octopus Tennis Undergrip on my students’ rackets.

It isn’t another overgrip.

It replaces the standard base grip underneath your normal overgrip.

The Octopus is made from flexible silicone with a raised, shock-absorbing structure.

When the racket vibrates after impact, the silicone bumps compress.

They help absorb that vibration before as much of it reaches your hand, wrist and elbow.

Then the silicone rebounds instead of remaining permanently flattened like ordinary foam.

You still wrap your favourite overgrip on top.

So you keep the tack, texture and surface feel you already prefer.

But underneath it, you have a more protective and responsive foundation.

That distinction is important.

Your overgrip helps you hold the racket.

Your undergrip helps manage what the racket sends back into your arm.

The first thing many players notice is comfort.

The racket feels less harsh when they make imperfect contact.

Off-centre shots don’t feel as aggressive through the handle.

Long hitting sessions become easier on the hand and forearm.

But comfort isn’t the only reason I recommend it.

When a racket feels harsh or unstable, players instinctively grip it harder.
They tighten their fingers.
Their wrist becomes rigid.
Their forearm stays tense through the swing.
They may not even realize they’re doing it.
But that tension affects performance.

A tight hand makes it harder for the racket head to flow naturally.
You lose acceleration.
You lose touch.
You become tentative on full swings.
And the more tired your arm becomes, the tighter you hold the racket.

It becomes a cycle:
The racket feels harsh.
You grip harder.
Your arm becomes more tense.
The racket feels even harsher.

A more comfortable and stable handle can help you trust the racket again.

You don’t need to squeeze it as though it’s about to fly out of your hand.
Your wrist can stay looser.
Your swing can remain smoother.

And you can focus on the ball instead of thinking about your elbow.

That is why my students don’t only tell me the racket feels more comfortable.

They often say they feel more confident accelerating through the shot.
They feel more connected to the handle.
They stop making constant adjustments between points.
They can play longer before their hand and forearm feel exhausted.
And they stop arriving at lessons with ice wrapped around their elbow.

The Octopus doesn’t teach technique.
It doesn’t replace proper coaching.
And it can’t turn a beginner into a professional player.

What it does is remove an unnecessary source of harshness between the racket and your arm.
That gives your technique a better platform.

Because good technique is much harder to maintain when you’re protecting a sore wrist.
It’s difficult to swing freely when you’re anticipating elbow discomfort.

And no coach can get your best tennis out of you if your main concern is simply finishing the session without pain.

The Octopus works with:
→ Any standard tennis racket
→ Any racket brand
→ Your preferred overgrip
→ Recreational and competitive setups
→ Players who want comfort without losing racket feel

Installation is simple.
Remove the old base grip.
Roll the Octopus undergrip onto the handle using the application tool.
Then wrap your usual overgrip over it.

You don’t have to change your racket.
You don’t have to abandon the overgrip you already love.
And you don’t have to make the handle feel excessively padded or disconnected.
You’re simply upgrading the hidden layer underneath.

This is especially worth considering if:
→ You’re over 35 and play regularly
→ Your wrist or elbow feels tired after tennis
→ Off-centre shots feel harsh through the handle
→ You’ve started wearing a wrist or elbow brace
→ You need more recovery time between sessions
→ You grip the racket tighter as you get tired
→ Your existing base grip feels flat, hard or compressed
→ You want to continue playing several times per week
→ Staying on the court matters more to you than buying another new racket

Most tennis products promise more spin.
More power.
More control.

Those benefits are easy to advertise.

But at a certain point in your tennis life, the most valuable performance benefit is different:
Being able to play again tomorrow.
Then again next week.
And again ten years from now.

Because the best racket setup isn’t only the one that helps you hit harder today.

It’s the one that helps you keep playing the sport you love.

If you’re serious about staying on the court, look beneath your overgrip.

The small impacts you barely notice today may be the reason you’re forced to play less in the future.

The Octopus Undergrip helps create a more comfortable, stable and shock-absorbing connection between your hand and the racket.
Same racket.
Same overgrip.
Same player.
But a much better foundation for the years ahead.

Try the Octopus Tennis Undergrip today:
👉 rocketgrip.com/products/tennis-undergrip

P.S. You don’t need to wait until your elbow becomes a serious problem. Equipment changes are most useful before discomfort forces you to stop playing.

P.P.S. The Octopus is installed beneath your regular overgrip. You keep the surface feel you already like while upgrading the cushioning and vibration management underneath.

P.P.P.S. The Octopus is not a medical treatment. Persistent wrist, elbow or forearm pain should be assessed by an appropriate medical professional.

Please STOP telling yourself it's just your age. I'm 37. If your feet feel worse after hockey than they used to, it might not be your skates. It's probably what's between your foot and the boot.

Buying thicker socks didn't fix it for me.

I've been playing beer league for over 15 years.

For the last two seasons, this is what my body kept telling me: "My feet go numb by the second period." "My ankles feel wrecked walking to the car after a game." "I get blisters no matter what socks I buy." "Maybe I'm just getting too old for this."

Before I gave up another Tuesday night, I actually looked at what was going on inside my skate.

I pulled my socks off after a game and looked at them properly for the first time in years.

Flat. Sweaty. Zero grip left — if they ever had any to begin with.

I'd bought new skates that year. Broke them in properly. Even tried different insoles. But the one thing actually touching my foot never changed.

That was the mistake.

A regular sock feels fine going on. Soft, familiar. But your foot needs to stay locked in one position inside that boot, stride after stride — and a regular sock doesn't grip anything. It just lets your foot move.

Every stride, force travels from your push-off, through your foot, into the boot. If your foot shifts even a little inside there, some of that force turns into friction instead of speed. Into blisters instead of power. Into your ankle working overtime just to keep you stable.

One shift isn't the problem. But a season is hundreds of shifts. My feet were absorbing all of it, every single game.

At first it was small. Feet feeling hot by the second period. Heel tender the next day. Then it became a pattern — double up on socks, lace tighter, tape my heel before every game, sit out the second half of back-to-backs.

I started saying no to games I used to say yes to.

I told myself it was age.

It wasn't. My skates weren't the problem. What was between my foot and the boot was.

Doubling up on socks tricked me for a while — feet felt padded again, problem solved, or so I thought. But it was the same ungripped surface underneath, just with an extra layer. Like putting a second bald tire on top of the first one. More rubber, same grip.

So I switched to RocketGrip Hockey Grip Socks.

They've got silicone grip zones right at the heel, ankle, and arch — the exact spots where my foot used to slide. Instead of a flat sock just sitting there, it actually grips the inside of the boot when I push off.

You put them on exactly like a normal sock. Same fit I'm used to. I just upgraded what's happening underneath.

First game wearing them, I noticed it on the hard stops — my foot just wasn't moving around in there anymore. No hot spot building by the second period. No taping my heel beforehand.

The part I didn't expect: I stopped lacing my skates so tight. I used to crank them down hard because my foot felt unstable — that was me compensating. Once my foot was actually locked in, I didn't need to strangle it with the laces on top. My feet don't go numb nearly as fast now.

I'm not going to tell you this turned me into a faster skater. It's not a replacement for skates that actually fit you, and it's not a medical fix. It's one less thing working against your foot every stride.

Once you're past 35, recovery matters as much as performance. The goal isn't just playing well tonight — it's still wanting to lace up next season, and in five years.

Nobody markets hockey gear around this. It's always more speed, more power, lighter equipment. For guys like me, the actual advantage is just being able to keep showing up — playing back-to-back nights, finishing a game without my ankle feeling wrecked, playing Tuesday and still wanting to play Thursday.

RocketGrip works with any skate, any brand, whatever fit you already play in — recreational or competitive. You just wear them like a normal sock and lace up the way you always do. No new skates, no new insoles, nothing to relearn.

Before you buy another pack of thick socks, before you blame your skates, before you decide sore feet are just the price of playing past 35 — pull off your sock after your next game and actually look at it.

It might still look fine. It might not be doing its job anymore.

STOP blaming your skates. Upgrade the layer that actually holds your foot in place.

Try RocketGrip Hockey Grip Socks: 👉 rocketgrip.com/products/custom-hockey-grip-socks

P.S. They go on just like a normal sock — same skates, same lacing, just a better foundation underneath.

P.P.S. Don't wait until sore feet or ankle instability start deciding how often you play. I wish I'd switched two seasons earlier.

P.P.P.S. Persistent foot, ankle, or joint pain should be assessed by an appropriate healthcare professional.

Please STOP putting a fresh overgrip on top of a dead base grip.

If you’re over 35 and your wrist or elbow feels worse after tennis than it used to, your racket may be sending far more vibration into your arm than you realize.

And replacing the overgrip won’t fix it.

I’ve coached tennis for over 20 years.

Whenever a player tells me:
“My elbow is starting to bother me.”
“My wrist feels beaten up after longer matches.”
“I can’t play two days in a row anymore.”
“I think I’m getting too old for tennis.”

I check one thing before we discuss a new racket, new strings or another brace.

I peel back their overgrip.

And underneath, I usually find the same thing.

A flattened, compressed base grip that stopped doing its job months—or even years—ago.

The player has replaced the outer grip ten times.

But the layer responsible for cushioning every impact has never been touched.

That’s the mistake.

Your overgrip is only the surface.
It gives you tack.
It absorbs sweat.
It makes the handle feel fresh.

But underneath that thin layer is the base grip sitting directly between your hand and the hard racket handle.

And every time you strike the ball, vibration travels:
From the strings…
Through the racket frame…
Down the handle…
Into your palm, wrist, forearm and elbow.

One shot isn’t the problem.

But tennis is not one shot.

It’s hundreds of impacts in a single session.
Thousands every month.
Year after year.

And when the foam beneath your overgrip becomes compressed, it absorbs less of that vibration.

So your arm absorbs more.

At first, you barely notice it.
Your forearm feels slightly tired after playing.
Your wrist is stiff the next morning.
Your elbow takes longer to warm up.

Then you begin making small adjustments.
You grip the racket tighter.
You avoid serving at full speed.
You stop hitting your backhand freely.
You wear a brace.
You ice your elbow after playing.
You take an extra day off between sessions.

Eventually, the player who once played four times per week is nervous about playing twice.

And they blame their age.

But the problem may not be that their body suddenly became incapable of tennis.

Their equipment may simply have stopped protecting them from the repeated impact.

That is why putting on another overgrip can be misleading.
The racket feels fresh again.
The handle feels tackier.

For a few sessions, you think the problem is solved.

But the same hard, compressed foundation is still sitting underneath.

It’s like putting a new mattress cover over a mattress that has completely collapsed.
The surface looks better.
The support underneath hasn’t changed.

That’s why I now recommend the Octopus Tennis Undergrip to players who are serious about staying on the court.

It replaces the standard foam base grip beneath your normal overgrip.

Instead of relying on foam that gradually flattens, the Octopus uses a flexible silicone structure with raised cushioning points.

When the racket vibrates after impact, the silicone compresses.

It helps absorb the vibration before as much of it reaches your arm.
Then it rebounds.
That rebound matters.

Traditional foam gradually becomes flatter and harder.

The silicone structure is designed to keep responding instead of simply staying compressed.

You then wrap your favourite overgrip on top.

So you don’t have to change the tack, texture or surface feel you already like.
You keep your normal overgrip.
You upgrade the hidden foundation beneath it.

The first time many players use it, they notice that the racket feels less harsh.
Especially on imperfect contact.
You know the shot.
You catch the ball slightly late.
Or too close to the frame.

The racket sends a sharp sensation directly into your hand.
With a better layer beneath the grip, that impact feels more controlled.
Less aggressive.
More cushioned without making the racket feel soft or disconnected.

But there’s another benefit players often don’t expect.

They stop squeezing the racket so hard.

When your handle feels unstable or harsh, your body naturally tries to protect itself.
Your fingers tighten.
Your wrist becomes rigid.
Your forearm stays tense through the swing.

That tension may help you feel secure for a moment.

But it can also reduce racket-head speed, touch and fluidity.
You start fighting the racket instead of swinging it.

A more comfortable and stable foundation helps you hold the handle securely without strangling it.
Your hand can stay looser.
Your wrist can move more naturally.
Your forearm doesn’t need to remain tense through every shot.
And your attention can return to the ball instead of the discomfort in your elbow.

This is not about turning you into a professional player.
It’s not a replacement for technique.

And it’s not a medical treatment.
It’s a simple equipment change designed to reduce one unnecessary source of stress between your racket and your arm.

Because once you reach your late 30s, 40s or 50s, recovery matters.

The goal isn’t only to play well today.

It’s to still be playing tomorrow.
Next season.
And ten years from now.

Most tennis marketing focuses on:
More spin.
More power.
More control.

But for many experienced players, the most valuable performance advantage is being able to keep showing up.
To finish a match without immediately reaching for the ice pack.
To serve freely instead of protecting the elbow.
To play on Saturday and still feel capable of playing again on Sunday.

That’s tennis longevity.

And it often starts with reducing the repeated stress your body absorbs from every shot.

The Octopus Undergrip works with:
→ Standard tennis rackets
→ Any racket brand
→ Your preferred overgrip
→ Recreational and competitive setups
→ Players who want more cushioning without losing feel

Installation is straightforward.
Remove the old base grip.
Roll the Octopus onto the racket handle using the included application tool.
Then wrap your normal overgrip over it.

You don’t need to buy a new racket.
You don’t need to change your strings.
You don’t need to abandon the grip texture you already prefer.
You simply replace the worn-out layer nobody thinks about.

So before you buy another pack of overgrips…

Before you blame your racket…

And before you decide that wrist and elbow discomfort are simply the price of getting older…

Look underneath.

Your overgrip may still look fine.

But the base grip beneath it may have stopped protecting you a long time ago.

STOP covering the problem with another overgrip.

Upgrade the layer that absorbs the impact.

Try the Octopus Tennis Undergrip:
👉 rocketgrip.com/products/tennis-undergrip

P.S. The Octopus sits beneath your regular overgrip. You keep the outer feel you already like while upgrading the cushioning and vibration management underneath.

P.P.S. Don’t wait until discomfort forces you to stop playing. The best time to protect your future years on the court is while you’re still able to enjoy them.

P.P.P.S. Persistent wrist, elbow or forearm pain should be assessed by an appropriate healthcare professional.

Please STOP blaming your skates for feet that go numb by the second period.

If you're over 35 and your feet feel worse after hockey than they used to, your skates probably aren't the problem. It's what's between your foot and the boot.

And a thicker pair of socks won't fix it.

I've coached hockey for over 20 years.

Whenever a player tells me: "My feet go numb by the second period." "My ankles feel wrecked by the third." "I get blisters no matter what socks I wear." "I think I'm getting too old to play three times a week."

I check one thing before we talk about new skates, new insoles, or another brace.

I ask what's actually on their foot.

And underneath the skate, I usually find the same thing.

A regular sock — cotton, basic athletic, whatever was in the drawer — that was never built to handle what happens inside a hockey boot.

The player has broken in two new pairs of skates. Tried different lacing. Added insoles. But the one layer that actually touches his foot has never changed.

That's the mistake.

Your sock feels soft. Familiar. Like a sock should.

But between your foot and the hard shell of the boot, your foot needs to stay locked in exactly one position, stride after stride. A regular sock doesn't grip anything. It just sits there — and lets your foot travel.

Every stride you take, force moves: From your push-off… Through your foot… Into the boot…

And if your foot shifts even a few millimeters inside that boot, some of that force doesn't go into your stride. It goes into friction. Into your skin. Into your ankle working overtime to stabilize what your sock isn't holding in place.

One stride isn't the problem.

But hockey is not one stride.

It's dozens of hard pushes in a single shift. Hundreds in a game. Thousands across a season.

And when your sock has zero grip, your foot moves a little more with every one of them. So your skin absorbs more. Your ankle works harder.

Please STOP putting a fresh overgrip on top of a dead base grip.

If you’re over 35 and your wrist or elbow feels worse after tennis than it used to, your racket may be sending far more vibration into your arm than you realize.

And replacing the overgrip won’t fix it.

I’ve coached tennis for over 20 years.

Whenever a player tells me:
“My elbow is starting to bother me.”
“My wrist feels beaten up after longer matches.”
“I can’t play two days in a row anymore.”
“I think I’m getting too old for tennis.”

I check one thing before we discuss a new racket, new strings or another brace.

I peel back their overgrip.

And underneath, I usually find the same thing.

A flattened, compressed base grip that stopped doing its job months—or even years—ago.

The player has replaced the outer grip ten times.

But the layer responsible for cushioning every impact has never been touched.

That’s the mistake.

Your overgrip is only the surface.
It gives you tack.
It absorbs sweat.
It makes the handle feel fresh.

But underneath that thin layer is the base grip sitting directly between your hand and the hard racket handle.

And every time you strike the ball, vibration travels:
From the strings…
Through the racket frame…
Down the handle…
Into your palm, wrist, forearm and elbow.

One shot isn’t the problem.

But tennis is not one shot.

It’s hundreds of impacts in a single session.
Thousands every month.
Year after year.

And when the foam beneath your overgrip becomes compressed, it absorbs less of that vibration.

So your arm absorbs more.

At first, you barely notice it.
Your forearm feels slightly tired after playing.
Your wrist is stiff the next morning.
Your elbow takes longer to warm up.

Then you begin making small adjustments.
You grip the racket tighter.
You avoid serving at full speed.
You stop hitting your backhand freely.
You wear a brace.
You ice your elbow after playing.
You take an extra day off between sessions.

Eventually, the player who once played four times per week is nervous about playing twice.

And they blame their age.

But the problem may not be that their body suddenly became incapable of tennis.

Their equipment may simply have stopped protecting them from the repeated impact.

That is why putting on another overgrip can be misleading.
The racket feels fresh again.
The handle feels tackier.

For a few sessions, you think the problem is solved.

But the same hard, compressed foundation is still sitting underneath.

It’s like putting a new mattress cover over a mattress that has completely collapsed.
The surface looks better.
The support underneath hasn’t changed.

That’s why I now recommend the Octopus Tennis Undergrip to players who are serious about staying on the court.

It replaces the standard foam base grip beneath your normal overgrip.

Instead of relying on foam that gradually flattens, the Octopus uses a flexible silicone structure with raised cushioning points.

When the racket vibrates after impact, the silicone compresses.

It helps absorb the vibration before as much of it reaches your arm.
Then it rebounds.
That rebound matters.

Traditional foam gradually becomes flatter and harder.

The silicone structure is designed to keep responding instead of simply staying compressed.

You then wrap your favourite overgrip on top.

So you don’t have to change the tack, texture or surface feel you already like.
You keep your normal overgrip.
You upgrade the hidden foundation beneath it.

The first time many players use it, they notice that the racket feels less harsh.
Especially on imperfect contact.
You know the shot.
You catch the ball slightly late.
Or too close to the frame.

The racket sends a sharp sensation directly into your hand.
With a better layer beneath the grip, that impact feels more controlled.
Less aggressive.
More cushioned without making the racket feel soft or disconnected.

But there’s another benefit players often don’t expect.

They stop squeezing the racket so hard.

When your handle feels unstable or harsh, your body naturally tries to protect itself.
Your fingers tighten.
Your wrist becomes rigid.
Your forearm stays tense through the swing.

That tension may help you feel secure for a moment.

But it can also reduce racket-head speed, touch and fluidity.
You start fighting the racket instead of swinging it.

A more comfortable and stable foundation helps you hold the handle securely without strangling it.
Your hand can stay looser.
Your wrist can move more naturally.
Your forearm doesn’t need to remain tense through every shot.
And your attention can return to the ball instead of the discomfort in your elbow.

This is not about turning you into a professional player.
It’s not a replacement for technique.

And it’s not a medical treatment.
It’s a simple equipment change designed to reduce one unnecessary source of stress between your racket and your arm.

Because once you reach your late 30s, 40s or 50s, recovery matters.

The goal isn’t only to play well today.

It’s to still be playing tomorrow.
Next season.
And ten years from now.

Most tennis marketing focuses on:
More spin.
More power.
More control.

But for many experienced players, the most valuable performance advantage is being able to keep showing up.
To finish a match without immediately reaching for the ice pack.
To serve freely instead of protecting the elbow.
To play on Saturday and still feel capable of playing again on Sunday.

That’s tennis longevity.

And it often starts with reducing the repeated stress your body absorbs from every shot.

The Octopus Undergrip works with:
→ Standard tennis rackets
→ Any racket brand
→ Your preferred overgrip
→ Recreational and competitive setups
→ Players who want more cushioning without losing feel

Installation is straightforward.
Remove the old base grip.
Roll the Octopus onto the racket handle using the included application tool.
Then wrap your normal overgrip over it.

You don’t need to buy a new racket.
You don’t need to change your strings.
You don’t need to abandon the grip texture you already prefer.
You simply replace the worn-out layer nobody thinks about.

So before you buy another pack of overgrips…

Before you blame your racket…

And before you decide that wrist and elbow discomfort are simply the price of getting older…

Look underneath.

Your overgrip may still look fine.

But the base grip beneath it may have stopped protecting you a long time ago.

STOP covering the problem with another overgrip.

Upgrade the layer that absorbs the impact.

Try the Octopus Tennis Undergrip:
👉 rocketgrip.com/products/tennis-undergrip

P.S. The Octopus sits beneath your regular overgrip. You keep the outer feel you already like while upgrading the cushioning and vibration management underneath.

P.P.S. Don’t wait until discomfort forces you to stop playing. The best time to protect your future years on the court is while you’re still able to enjoy them.

P.P.P.S. Persistent wrist, elbow or forearm pain should be assessed by an appropriate healthcare professional.
